I own L3 for these services, so I've spent real time on what happens when firmware, flaky cell links, and a protocol spec that vendors each implement creatively all meet in production.

The most interesting thing I've fixed recently: a Node.js Kafka consumer doing fire-and-forget processing with no concurrency limit. Most recently, I have been the technical lead and one of the earliest engineers at Siift, where I built and now own much of the core platform behind a production AI product. I designed the persistent runtime coordinating 50+ specialized agents, typed tools, approval gates, scheduled actions, retries, recovery, and mutations against live product state. I also built the real-time SSE infrastructure and the multi-tenant data architecture behind conversations, research, sources, project state, generated assets, memory, and long-running workflows.

My ownership at Siift extends across the full product: backend services, agent architecture, frontend systems, authentication, teams and sharing, connectors, search, analytics, data modelling, caching, observability, deployment, AWS infrastructure, production debugging, and technical direction. I work directly with the founder on product and architecture decisions, then carry those decisions through implementation and production.

Before Siift, I worked directly with the CTO at GenRAIT to take a genomic data platform from requirements to production. I built resumable Go ingestion pipelines, integrity validation, retries, reconciliation, persisted job state, biological data models, metadata and expression-level search, and distributed-storage integrations.

At RentAHuman, I worked alongside the founder and Stripe’s integration team to build the initial payments infrastructure for a live marketplace with roughly 600,000 users. I owned authorization, manual capture, platform fees, payouts, refunds, disputes, warranty holds, webhook-driven state transitions, idempotency, reconciliation, messaging, and customer-support workflows.

I also lead the ongoing modernization of a live manufacturing ERP covering inventory, production, costing, quotations, logistics, invoicing, and exports. That work involves reverse-engineering legacy C#, VB.NET, MSSQL, and ASP.NET systems and replacing them incrementally with modular .NET and FastAPI services, PostgreSQL, Redis, Docker, and React without disrupting active business operations.

Outside of work, I am building NullDown, a persistent document, application, and memory substrate where humans and AI agents can operate against the same structured state. It supports snapshot-based persistence, structured mutations, indexed retrieval, conflict-safe co-authoring, embedded data, and projection into interactive interfaces.

I am looking for founding engineer, technical lead, full-stack, backend, and platform engineering roles. I am equally open to a strong full-stack engineering role where I can take substantial ownership and grow into or directly carry technical leadership. Across my recent work, I have already owned architecture, implementation, infrastructure, deployment, production operations, and technical product decisions across AI systems, payments, data platforms, and enterprise software.

Lawyer-technologist designing and building agentic AI systems for legal and other high-stakes work. I focus on the difficult distance between a promising demo and a deployment-ready workflow: selecting the right work, mapping privilege, data, and authority boundaries, designing evals and human-decision gates, and creating tool-agnostic operating architectures that can survive legal and security review. Current obsession: chaining authority- and scope-bounded agents into high-assurance workflows that can run autonomously for six-plus hours, show their receipts, and stop at explicit human (sometimes licensed professional) gates between stages—then produce genuinely valuable, substantial, compliant, and defensible deliverables.

A useful first engagement is a bounded two-week sprint: rank workflows by value, readiness, and fit; sketch an initial target operating architecture; and produce a prioritized 90-day pilot plan plus one implementation-ready pilot brief.

I have been shipping software for twenty years, most of it Rails, and what I own has always run wider than the code I write. The work starts in a room where most of the people are not engineers and the problem has not been named yet, and it carries through the data model, the API contract, the authorization boundary, the background queues, the deploy, and whoever holds the pager afterward. Being accountable across that whole span is a broader claim than full stack, and a harder one to fake.

The depth sits in Rails and Postgres, where I have built async pipelines that had to survive real traffic, payments and third-party integrations that could not quietly drop money, and authorization models that grew more intricate every quarter as the business kept inventing new kinds of users. I reach for Hotwire when the product needs a face, run Docker daily, and treat application security as ordinary hygiene rather than a phase, which means reading the CVEs that touch my stack, running Brakeman and bundler-audit, and reviewing changes against OWASP before they land.

I work with agents every day and skeptically, on the same practice I was using before the tooling existed: discovery before implementation, verification before reference, scope control before anything ships.

Two of the more interesting systems I built are ones I argued to shut down, once the numbers showed they cost more than they were worth, and I wrote up the reasoning both times so the decision outlived the project. That judgment matters more to me than shipping volume, because I would rather be right in month three than committed in month nine.

I am looking for senior IC, staff, or principal work on a team with clear direction and problems worth the depth, whether that runs toward Rails and backend architecture, greenfield systems design, or LLM work that has to earn its place in the product. Available now.

What that covered: the live captioning pipeline, where latency, accuracy, and reliability all had to hold at once. Drove the backend from a monolith into a monolith plus microservices plus serverless, over an event-driven layer, to keep service stable. An observability stack with Prometheus and Grafana, built from scratch. A datastore migration across 100K+ accounts with no downtime, running both databases live instead of taking a batch window. How I work: most of what I've built started as a vague idea, and my job was making it specific enough for other teams to build against. I own my scope end to end, and once people start building, the spec always changes. That back-and-forth is where the design actually gets figured out.

My first AI reviewer scored well on my own gold set and near zero on the external W3C one, because it shared a rubric with the drafter. A second reviewer reading independently now catches 53% of those errors. Small-sample measurements, not proof.

VOX Personalis: fine-tuned Whisper with LoRA on my own Deaf-accented speech, because no off-the-shelf ASR handles it. WER 238.69% to 34.05%, now with sub-second streaming output. Next is sub-20% and on-device.

I build data pipelines that know when they're lying to you.

GAScout (https://gascout.pages.dev) — Georgia public-records pipeline. Four counties live, each a different ingestion problem resolved into one schema: a 9,915-page fixed-width mainframe PDF (409,142 records, zero dropped rows), a weekly XLSX roll, monthly text PDFs, and scanned sheriff's levy documents via OCR. Adding a county is a config file, not code. The other 155 are labeled planned rather than filled with invented numbers.

FindStorage (https://findstorage.pages.dev) — national self-storage pricing tracker. 4,639 locations, 245,000+ price changes logged, running unattended on a daily schedule. Aborts rather than publishing when the store count moves more than it should, because the failure that costs you isn't a crash — it's a scraper quietly returning less after a site changes and nobody noticing for three weeks.

Also built a WiFi CSI device-fingerprinting array on ESP32 — custom ESP-IDF firmware and a Python DSP pipeline, running as my apartment's security system. Cross-manufacturer separation holds at 11-15 sigma; same-model discrimination tops out near 77% and true clock twins are the open problem.

Before this I ran a 500-acre motocross park in Northern California: acquired dormant land, re-entitled it, directed a 120-person race-day crew, ran the medical plan through a mid-event helicopter evacuation, and sold my stake.

Self-taught, ~18 months in. Interested in data engineering, pipeline work, and anything where messy real-world sources have to become trustworthy structured data.
